newsitem.title: VATICAN: Vatican confirms papal trip to Cuba in Jan 1998.
newsitem.headline: Vatican confirms papal trip to Cuba in Jan 1998.

text.p: Pope John Paul will make his planned historic visit to communist-ruled Cuba in the second half of January 1998, the Vatican confirmed on Saturday.
It issued a statement after an announcement in Havana by Cuban Cardinal Jaime Ortega that the trip, initially expected to take place this year, would go ahead next January.
"As announced last night in Havana, I can confirm that the Holy Father will make a pastoral visit to Cuba in the second half of January 1998," chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said.
It will be the first visit by the Pope, a crusader against communism, to the Caribbean island, the only Spanish-speaking country in Latin America which he has not visited.

President Fidel Castro invited the Pope to Cuba during a ground-breaking audience at the Vatican last November which highlighted a thaw in relations between the island's communist authorities and the Roman Catholic Church.
Both sides said then that no conditions had been attached to the visit and that they hoped it could take place some time in 1997.

The 76-year-old Pontiff, who has suffered a string of health problems in recent years and had his appendix removed last October, already has four foreign trips planned for 1997 and has been advised by doctors to reduce his workload.
This year's trips are to Prague, his native Poland, Paris and Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The latter trip, in October, had prompted speculation that a stop in Cuba could be tagged on.
Ortega said in his statement that it would have been too hasty to organise a papal trip for the first half of 1997, adding the hot Cuban summer was not suitable for a visit.
It had also been agreed that the Pope's trip should not be tacked onto another visit, but should be a journey exclusively to the island, Ortega added.

"The Holy Father wants to visit our country and he would have liked to do so before the end of 1997, but the Christmas festival and other festivals around this time oblige him to postpone his visit to Cuba until January 1998," Ortega said.
The meeting between Castro and the Pope, and the announcement that the Pope would visit Cuba marked a clear improvement in recent months in ties.
The head of the Italian Church's bishops' conference, Cardinal Camillo Ruini, is visiting Cuba and met Castro on Friday afternoon, Cuban state media reported.
Ruini's visit included talks on the timing of a papal trip.

Shortly after Castro took power in 1959, Cuba was declared a socialist state. Some 350 Catholic schools were nationalised and more than 100 priests expelled. Freedom of worship and religious instruction are limited to church premises.

Although authorities have sought since the late 1980s to show more tolerance toward the island's Christian churches, tensions with the Roman Catholic church persisted, partly over periodic criticism of the political system by bishops.
Such tensions have eased recently, although Church officials continue to ask to play a wider public role in Cuba.
At the same time, the Church has delighted Castro by criticising sanctions imposed on the island by the United States to try to force the veteran revolutionary from power.
